pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–10 years

- **Topic:** Building an energy-converting device

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, England):** no general KS2 'energy' topic, so no direct UK science statutory match; the design-make-evaluate element lives in UK Design & Technology, and the science reasoning is anchored on KS2 'Working scientifically' (and Y6 Electricity for the electrical examples).

- **Standards — US NATIONAL (NGSS):** 4-PS3-4 (verbatim) '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-4]' (an engineering PE, asterisked); clarification gives examples (electric circuit → motion/light/sound; passive solar heater → heat) and constraints (materials, cost, time); assessment boundary limits devices to converting motion↔electric energy or using stored energy to cause motion/light/sound. NGSS-anchored. Builds on 'How energy travels' (transfer by sound/light/heat/electric current).

- **Operational details:** An ENGINEERING-DESIGN topic: children design, build, TEST and REFINE a simple device that converts energy from one carrier/store to another (e.g. a battery-and-buzzer that turns stored chemical energy into sound, a torch that makes light, a solar heater that turns sunlight into warmth, a windmill that turns moving air into motion). The science is qualitative — name the input and output — and the heart of the task is the design→test→improve cycle, NOT efficiency calculations or formulas. Honest framing per the modern model: every device TRANSFERS energy from a starting store to a useful output (it does not make energy from nothing); NGSS itself notes 'produce energy' really means converting stored energy into a useful form.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/procedural, age 9-10).
bestPractices: Make it a genuine design cycle, not a craft: define the goal and constraints (materials/time), build a first version, TEST it against the goal, then identify one improvement and rebuild — the refine step is the learning, so plan time for at least one iteration.

Anchor each device in a clear input→output energy story the child can state: 'stored chemical energy in the battery → sound from the buzzer' / 'sunlight → warmth in the dark cup' — naming the start store and the useful output.

Use the everyday 'form' words as the on-ramp but keep the honest message that the device TRANSFERS energy from a starting store (battery, wound elastic, sunlight, moving air) — it never creates energy — so children don't build a 'free energy' mental model.
Test with a measurable-enough goal (does the buzzer sound? how far does the car go? how warm did the water get?) so 'what works well / what to improve' is evidence-based, not opinion.
Surface that not all the input becomes the useful output — some spreads to the surroundings (the motor gets warm, some light is wasted) — named simply, with efficiency/Sankey deferred to KS3/HS.
keyRepresentations: An input→device→output energy-flow strip for the chosen device (e.g. battery [chemical] → motor → wheels [motion]).
A design-loop diagram: design → build → test → refine → (test again), making iteration explicit.
A test-and-improve record: goal, what happened, one change to try next.

Concrete buildables: battery+buzzer (sound), battery+bulb (light), battery+motor car (motion), wound-elastic or rubber-band racer (elastic→motion), black-cup passive solar heater (light→heat), simple windmill (moving air→motion).
commonMisconceptions: 'The device makes/produces energy' from nothing — it converts a starting store (battery, sunlight, wound spring); name the input every time to break the free-energy idea.
'Energy changes form' taken literally as a substance morphing — reframe as energy TRANSFERRED from one store/carrier to another, so KS3 store-and-pathway teaching isn't undermined.
Expecting 100% of the input to become the useful output — some always spreads to the surroundings (warmth, wasted light/sound); kept qualitative here.
Treating the FIRST build as the finished answer — missing that test-and-refine (iteration) is the point of the task.
Confusing 'it works' with 'it meets the goal/constraints' — a device can run but still fail the brief (too slow, uses too much, wrong output).

learn.summary: For ages 9–10, children apply scientific ideas to design, build, [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-4] a starting source into a useful output (e.g. battery+buzzer for sound, battery+bulb for light, battery+motor car for motion, wound-elastic racer, black-cup passive solar heater, simple windmill). The science stays qualitative — name the input (e.g. a battery, wound elastic, sunlight or moving air) and the useful output — and the heart of the task is the design→test→refine cycle under real constraints (materials, time), not efficiency formulas. The honest framing is that a device TRANSFERS energy from a starting store or carrier to a useful output (some always spreads to the surroundings); it never creates energy. A hands-on build kit is the authentic home for this objective; a screen design-bench is a companion for rehearsing the energy-flow reasoning and the iteration loop, and a cutaway reference or matching/sequence task supports naming and consolidation.

activities.title: Design, build and refine a real energy-converting device
feedback: If a learner describes the device as 'making' movement or light, ask what went IN to make that happen and trace the chain back to the source (chemical energy in the battery, elastic energy you wound in, sunlight falling on the cup) — nothing is created.

If a learner names only the output ('it buzzes', 'it lights up'), prompt 'where did the energy for that come from?' to draw out the full input→output chain, and have them point to the part where the energy is transferred to the output.
If a learner swaps parts at random when it underperforms, ask what exactly is going wrong first, then change one thing and re-test — model fair, targeted iteration.
Ask: could the device run forever without the battery, or without re-winding it? Use the 'no' to reinforce that the energy comes from a finite starting store or an ongoing supply like sunlight.
Prompt: is any energy going somewhere you didn't intend, like heat or sound? Not all the input becomes the useful output.
activities.rationale: 4-PS3-4 is an engineering-design performance expectation requiring children to design, test, and refine a real device under constraints of materials, cost and time; the deepest learning at this age is the hands-on iteration (the motor too weak, the elastic that snaps, the cup that warms only in sun). Naming the energy source every time and refusing a device with no source counter the common 'device makes energy' idea.
sourceClaims: 4-PS3-4 verbatim ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-4]'); clarification examples (electric circuit→motion/light/sound; passive solar heater→heat) and constraints (materials, cost, time); DCI PS3.D "'[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-4]"; assessment boundary limits devices to motion↔electric or stored-energy→motion/light/sound.
Children commonly think a device 'makes' energy and that all input becomes useful output; the honest model is energy transferred from a starting store with some spreading to the surroundings.
learnerActions: Take a design brief with a measurable-enough goal, e.g. 'make the buggy cross this line', 'warm the water in the cup', or 'make the buzzer sound'.

Choose an energy source and a matching converter from real kit: a battery with a motor, bulb or buzzer; a wound elastic band turning an axle and wheels; sunlight on a black cup (or foil reflector); or moving air turning windmill blades; plus parts (wheels, card, black cup, foil).
Build a first version, then TEST it against the goal and record what actually happened (did it cross the line? how far? how warm?).
State the energy story out loud: name where the energy starts and the useful output, e.g. 'stored chemical energy in the battery → the motor turns → the wheels move'.
Identify ONE specific weakness from the test evidence, change just that one thing (fresher/bigger source, lighter load), and re-test to see if it improved.

Point to the part where the energy is transferred to the useful output (e.g. the motor, where the electric current makes it spin), and name any energy that spread to the surroundings (e.g. the motor got warm, or some light or sound was wasted).
activities.intendedInsight: A device moves energy from a starting source to a useful output — it never makes energy from nothing — and the first build is meant to be improved: targeted test-and-refine, not random tinkering, is the point of the task.

activities.title: On-screen design-bench to rehearse the energy flow and the refine loop
feedback: When the first run stops short, prompt the learner to name the observed weakness before changing anything, then change one variable and re-test.
Use the refused 'no source' run to ask aloud 'where would the energy come from?' and connect back to real starting sources.
When the energy-flow strip shows a 'to surroundings' leak, point out that not all the input becomes the useful output.
activities.rationale: A live-state design sandbox may make the design→test→refine loop and the input→output energy flow visible and lets a learner change one thing and re-test, which is intended to support the reasoning half of the engineering task. It is proposed as a companion to, not a replacement for, the physical build; its effectiveness relative to the real kit is untested.
sourceClaims: 4-PS3-4 verbatim ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-4]'); clarification examples (electric circuit→motion/light/sound; passive solar heater→heat) and constraints (materials, cost, time); DCI PS3.D "'[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS3-4]"; assessment boundary limits devices to motion↔electric or stored-energy→motion/light/sound.
Children commonly think a device 'makes' energy and that all input becomes useful output; the honest model is energy transferred from a starting store with some spreading to the surroundings.
learnerActions: Pick an energy source from a palette (battery, wound elastic, or a sunbeam) and snap it to a converter and load that can use it (e.g. battery to motor, bulb or buzzer; wound elastic to an axle and wheels; sunbeam to a black cup of water); a pairing that cannot work, such as a sunbeam straight to a motor with no solar cell, should not run.
Take a goal card (e.g. 'make the car cross the line' / 'warm the water') and run the test.
Watch the input→output energy-flow strip light up (e.g. battery [chemical] → motor → wheels [motion]) and note the small 'to surroundings' leak as the motor warms.
When the buggy crawls halfway and stops, use a refine panel to change ONE thing — swap to a bigger source or a lighter load — and re-test, with each attempt logged so the iteration is visible.
Try building a device with NO energy source and see the bench refuse to run ('where is the energy coming from?').
activities.intendedInsight: The device only ever moves energy from a starting source to a useful output, the first try is meant to be improved, and a device with no energy source cannot do anything — there is no free energy.

activities.title: Cutaway reference: name the input→output story of real devices
feedback: If a learner gives only the output, prompt them to add the starting source and the converter step so the full chain is spoken.
Ask which part is the energy source and which is the useful output for each device.
activities.rationale: A cutaway reference is a support for the naming half of the topic and for consolidation; by itself it does not elicit the design, test or refine actions that are the core of the engineering objective, so it should be used alongside building, not instead of it.
learnerActions: Explore a tappable cutaway of real devices (torch, buzzer car, solar heater).
For each, read out its energy story, e.g. tap a torch → 'chemical (battery) → electrical → light'.
Compare devices and say which starting source and which useful output each uses.
activities.intendedInsight: Every device has a nameable energy story: a starting source feeding through a converter to a useful output.

activities.title: Consolidation: match devices to conversions and order the design loop
feedback: For a matching error, prompt the learner to say the energy story aloud and re-check the starting source.
If the loop is mis-ordered, ask what you must do before you can refine something (build and test it first).
activities.rationale: A matching-and-sequencing task can check understanding of conversions and the design-loop order, but it assesses recognition and ordering and does not itself elicit the independent build-test-refine construction the objective requires.
learnerActions: Match each device to its input→output conversion (device → conversion).
Put the steps of the design loop in order: design → build → test → refine.
Answer 'where does the energy come from?' style questions, choosing the starting source.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure recall that devices convert from a named source, and that engineering follows a repeating design→build→test→refine loop.

constraints: Keep the science qualitative at this age: name the input (starting store or carrier) and the useful output; defer efficiency calculations, Sankey diagrams and formulas to later stages.

Make it a genuine design cycle, not a craft project: define goal and constraints, build, test against the goal, identify one improvement, and rebuild — plan time for at least one iteration, since the refine step is the learning.
Test against a measurable-enough goal (does the buzzer sound? how far did the car go? how warm did the water get?) so 'what works / what to improve' is evidence-based, not opinion.
Always name where the energy starts so children do not build a 'free energy' mental model; a device transfers energy, it does not create it.
Reframe 'energy changes form' as energy transferred from one store or carrier to another, so later store-and-pathway teaching is not undermined.
Surface simply that not all the input becomes the useful output — some spreads to the surroundings (warmth, wasted light/sound) — kept qualitative.

The screen design-bench, cutaway reference and matching/sequence tasks are companions for reasoning and consolidation; the explicit engineering objective (NGSS 4-PS3-4) needs a real build kit (cells, motors, buzzers, bulbs, wheels, elastic, black cups/foil) with a design brief and a test-and-refine sheet. Recognition and ordering tasks do not elicit independent construction.
Distinguish 'it works' from 'it meets the goal/constraints': a device can run but still fail the brief (too slow, uses too much, wrong output).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Standards framing: NGSS 4-PS3-4 is cited as verified in the source; the IOP Spark 'stores and pathways / energy dissipates' claim was marked verified:false in the original record and is retained but flagged, not treated as confirmed evidence. The UK framing (no general KS2 energy topic; design-make-evaluate in D&T; reasoning in Working Scientifically; electrical examples in Y6 Electricity) is retained as stated but not independently checked here.

The row's input list treats sunlight and moving air as 'stores'. In the stores-and-pathways model the kinetic energy of moving air is itself a store, while radiation (sunlight) is a pathway/carrier. Learner-facing text uses the generic 'starting store or carrier' and lists the four example inputs without bucketing moving air as a carrier, while preserving the age-appropriate simplification.

The original labelled a hands-on 3D build as adding 'handling cost without conceptual gain', which conflicts with the stated catalog gap that the standard requires a real built-and-refined device. Resolved: the physical build is the authentic objective; the digital bench and reference/matching tasks are proposed companions of untested relative effectiveness.

Catalog-ranking language ('ideal/possible/poor fit', '3D adds nothing', 'not recommended' for dialogue) and internal IDs (including the reteach-prerequisite pointer mt_X_aDUBh-HF) were removed; the misconception reteach step is retained conceptually in feedback, and objective affordance/limit statements are kept without treating any medium as universally superior.

probeDeeper: What form of energy goes into your device, and what form comes out? Is any energy going somewhere you didn't intend, like heat or sound?
When it didn't work as well as you wanted, how did you decide what to change?
Could your device run forever without the battery, or without you winding it up again? Why not?
Point to the exact part of your device where one form of energy becomes another.
assess.correctAnswer: The child builds a working device (e.g. battery → motor spinning a card fan: chemical → electrical → kinetic; or a plucked elastic band across a box: kinetic → sound), tests it, identifies a specific weakness, makes one purposeful change that improves it, and correctly names the energy conversion at each stage — including energy that ends up as unwanted heat or sound.

errorPatterns.pattern: Device 'makes' energy: describes the device as creating movement/light out of nothing, omitting the input store (the battery, the winding, the push).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask what went IN to make the output happen; trace the chain back to the store (chemical energy in the battery, elastic energy you put in) — nothing is created.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The spoken conversion account has an output form but no input source — energy appears from the device itself.

errorPatterns.pattern: Names only the output, not the conversion: says 'it makes light' or 'it buzzes' but not that electrical energy is being converted into light/sound.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach: prompt 'what turned into that?' to draw out the full chain; have them point to where the conversion happens.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When explaining, gives the end result without the input→output chain, though the child does know energy comes in forms.

errorPatterns.pattern: Untargeted trial and error: when the device underperforms, changes parts at random rather than the part that isn't working.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask what exactly is going wrong before changing anything, then change one thing and re-test — model fair, targeted iteration.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: During the improve step, swaps or adjusts components with no link to the observed weakness.

responseLevels.gap: Assembles parts without a working conversion, or cannot say what turns into what; talks as if the device makes energy.
responseLevels.full: Designs and builds a working converter, names the energy conversion at each stage (including unintended heat or sound), tests it, and makes a purposeful change aimed at the identified weakness — coordinating design, energy analysis, and iteration, and transferring the reasoning to a different conversion.
responseLevels.partial: Builds something that works and names the final form ('it lights up'), and tinkers when it fails, but cannot state the full conversion chain (input → output) or target improvements at the actual weak point.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Using these materials — a small motor, a battery and wires, card, elastic bands, a buzzer and a bulb — design and build a device that turns one form of energy into another (for example electrical energy into movement, or movement into sound). Build it, test whether it works, then change one thing to make it work better. As you go, tell me what form of energy is turning into what. I'll watch rather than help.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the build separates a child who understands energy conversion — names the input and output forms, and targets the improvement at the actual weak point — from one who assembles by trial and error and can only name the final form. The quality of the iteration and the spoken conversion chain reveal the understanding; a verbal description of a procedure would not.
